30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 21: Week 3 Wrap-Up — Skills, Subagents, or MCP? How to Choose
Somehow we've already made it to the end of Week 3.
So this post pulls together the three ways we've covered for extending and powering up the AI — Skills, subagents, and MCP — so you're less confused about which one to reach for in practice.
Over the past week we met Skills, subagents, and MCP one at a time, and each of them has its own job:

: Teaches the AI a method or workflow, so it does things the way you expect. Like the commit-message Skill we used earlier, where we taught the AI how to write commit messages, or bringing in the Frontend Design rules so the AI knows how the front-end UI should be designed.
: You spend money (tokens) to hire a specialist for a specific job. Like the code-reviewer subagent from earlier — we hired a specialist to review our code and report the results back to us.

: A universal adapter that lets the AI talk to things outside your project. Like when we used Context7 MCP, we let the AI look up official docs directly. You can also hook it up to external tools like GitHub or Figma, so the AI can talk to them directly.

There's one thing I really want to stress here: these three aren't mutually exclusive. They work together. Picking a Skill doesn't mean you can't use MCP, and picking a subagent doesn't mean you can't use a Skill. Don't forget the Context7 MCP example from earlier — it used a Skill and a Rule at the same time. MCP handled looking up the docs, while the Skill and the Rule told the AI when it should go look things up. That's a real example of stacking several of these together.
Now that you know what each one is for, the next step is figuring out how to choose.
Basically, you can use these three questions to decide what to use and when:
Is this the same approach you'll reuse over and over?
If yes, write a Skill. Anything you have to do every single time can become a Skill — like the commit message format, front-end UI design rules, the steps for looking up official docs, and so on.
Is this work you could hand off and just get the conclusion back?

If yes, create a subagent. Work that eats up a lot of Context — like code review, research, or scanning a big chunk of the project — is a great fit for a subagent. Let it finish the job and report the results back to you.
Does it need to touch anything outside the project folder?
If yes, hook up an MCP. Things like the browser, an internal database, Figma, GitHub, and so on all belong to the world outside your project folder, and that's when you need MCP.

So what if, as luck would have it, it's none of the three? Then just write a rule in CLAUDE.md. After all, CLAUDE.md is exactly the place for rules that can't be figured out just by reading the code.

But I think what we've covered so far handles about 80% of use cases. The remaining 20% you can pick up gradually through real-world work, or go looking for when you need it.
